question:
A hospitalized 71-year-old male with a history of hypertension and severe chronic obstructive
pulmonary disease shows a significant blood pressure elevation on his second day of admission for
cellulitis. His hypertension has been managed with hydrochlorothiazide for 10 years, and his COPD is
treated with inhaled fluticasone-salmeterol and tiotropium. He had a COPD exacerbation requiring
hospitalization one month prior. His admission blood pressure was 160/88 mm Hg, but is now 205/112
mm Hg with a heart rate of 88 beats per minute. Physical examination reveals clear lungs, regular
cardiac rhythm without murmurs or gallops, and no jugular venous distention. Fundoscopic
examination is normal without exudates or papilledema. He is mentally alert with no peripheral edema
or complaints of chest pain or dyspnea. Laboratory results show normal serum creatinine (1.1 mg/dL),
normal troponin, and urinalysis without proteinuria or hematuria. His electrocardiogram shows only
previously documented nonspecific ST-T-wave changes. What is the most appropriate management
strategy for this patient? Answer Choices: (A) Administer intravenous sodium nitroprusside (B) Add oral
clonidine (C) Initiate intravenous labetalol (D) Start oral hydralazine (E) Increase hydrochlorothiazide
dose (F) Administer sublingual nifedipine (G) Prescribe oral amlodipine (H) Add oral metoprolol (I)
Begin intravenous enalaprilat (J) Continue current therapy and monitor
 A. Administer sublingual nifedipine
B. Administer intravenous sodium nitroprusside
C. Prescribe oral amlodipine
